clue.text: Little money paid for underwear with little hesitation

parts.note: smalls is a British informal word for underwear
um is the short noise of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A trifling sum handed over for a pair of underpants, bought with barely a pause.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sum is a modest amount of cash, a pittance.

clue.text: Pulls up grass

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for pulls is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to draw is to pull

explanation.surface: Someone tugging tufts of turf out of a lawn.
explanation.definitionFit: Sward is an old word for a stretch of turf or grassy ground.

clue.text: Play the fool when there's a song in the air

definitions.text: when there's a song in the air

explanation.surface: Someone clowning around while music fills the room.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is whimsical: a skylark singing overhead means there is a lark about.
explanation.definitionFit: To clown around is to behave playfully; and a singing skylark nearby means one of those birds is around.

clue.text: A jumper who is perspiring

explanation.surface: A woolly pullover worn by someone already dripping with sweat.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted pullover is a jumper in British usage; and someone giving off perspiration is literally one who sweats.

clue.text: Rake tried modern cocktail-but he won't get drunk

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A rakish man tries a new cocktail but insists he will stay sober.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who drinks only in moderation is a restrained imbiber who stays sober.

clue.text: Prince enters diocese church for the address

indicators.note: the letter for prince goes inside the word for diocese

parts.note: a see is a bishop's diocese

explanation.surface: A royal arrives at the cathedral to deliver a talk.
explanation.definitionFit: An address is a formal talk given to an audience.

clue.text: He got Antonio embarrassed over security installation

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the word for embarrassed above the next piece

parts.note: shy means bashful or embarrassed
a lock is a device fitted for security

explanation.surface: A man who caught out Antonio is abashed about fitting a security device.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock is the moneylender in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice who holds Antonio to his bond.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's moneylender had the merchant in his power through the bond.

clue.text: The visible extent of King Harold's injury

explanation.surface: How far one can see, and the wound of England's last Saxon king.
explanation.walkthrough: King Harold II is traditionally said to have died at Hastings in 1066 from an arrow in the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeshot is the range of one's sight; and Harold was famously struck by an arrow in the eye.

clue.text: How dreams represented the expatriate's orientation

indicators.note: presented again in another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Dreams that reveal where an exile longs to be.
explanation.definitionFit: An exile's heart faces towards the native land, the direction of going back.

clue.text: Anti prose?

explanation.surface: A one-word question about whether writing in prose is against something.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer as A-VERSE: prose is non-verse, as if 'a-' meant 'not'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being opposed to something means being against it; and prose is jokingly the opposite of poetry.

clue.text: Fancy the idea of a siesta

explanation.surface: Someone liking the thought of an afternoon nap.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy is a reverie or flight of imagination; and a siesta is a daytime sleep, so its dreams are day ones.

clue.text: A bottle of wine can't be put into venison

indicators.note: the word goes inside the meat word

parts.note: venison is the meat of deer
taken without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A cook declaring a bottle of wine cannot go in the venison stew.
explanation.definitionFit: A decanter is a glass vessel into which wine is poured for serving.

clue.text: Exhibited son who made good

indicators.note: the letters are remade into a proper word

explanation.surface: A son who became a success is put on display.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on display is being exhibited to the public.

clue.text: King of the road!

parts.note: a ruler with absolute power whose realm is motoring: a car-ruler

explanation.surface: A driver who rules the highway.
explanation.definitionFit: An absolute ruler, here punningly an automobile despot.

clue.text: Excellent German money I invested in farming land

indicators.note: money is invested, so these letters are put inside the land word

parts.note: arable land is ploughed for crops
DM is the Deutschmark, Germany's former currency

explanation.surface: A fine idea: putting German cash and one's own into farmland.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worthy of high praise is excellent.

clue.text: Good order for a highland costumier

explanation.surface: A Scottish outfitter keeping everything neat.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in kilter means in proper working order; and one who makes kilts for Highlanders would be a kilt-maker.

clue.text: Member is not in time to conduct parliamentary business

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
taken as written
late means after the appointed time

explanation.surface: An MP who turns up late for a parliamentary sitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament's business is making laws.

clue.text: Never mind — it doesn't

parts.note: the phrase completed after 'it doesn't' gives the familiar reassurance that something is unimportant

explanation.surface: A shrug of reassurance: don't worry, it's of no importance.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is of no consequence means it has no importance or significance.

clue.text: It's hoisted as a result of operations in the rear

indicators.note: the operations word sits inside the rear word

parts.note: the tail is the rear end
ops is short for operations

explanation.surface: Something lifted after surgery on the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A topsail is a sail set above the lowest one, raised up the mast.

clue.text: Jack goes in to take a breather and begin again

indicators.note: the sailor word is placed inside the word for a breather

parts.note: to rest is to take a break
jack and tar are both slang for a sailor

explanation.surface: A man named Jack pops inside for a break before starting over.
explanation.definitionFit: To start something afresh is to resume it from the beginning.

clue.text: Long drinks for men on board

explanation.surface: Sailors on a ship downing big drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Draughts is the British name for the board game checkers; its pieces are 'men'.
explanation.definitionFit: Draughts are deep swallows of drink; and the counters in the board game checkers are its pieces.

clue.text: Commend a parish priest confronting old archbishop

parts.note: William Laud was Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I

explanation.surface: Praising a village vicar who stands up to a former archbishop.
explanation.definitionFit: To commend someone is to praise them publicly, as clapping does.

clue.text: Canoeists shoot them quietly during attacks

indicators.note: the letter for quietly falls within the word for attacks

parts.note: raids are attacks
P is piano, musical notation for quietly

explanation.surface: Paddlers firing silently in the middle of an assault.
explanation.definitionFit: White-water paddlers ride fast stretches of river, which is called shooting them.

clue.text: Grand declaration of the working model

explanation.surface: An impressive statement from a fashion model at work.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is 'I'm posing', what an artist's model at work might say.
explanation.definitionFit: Imposing means grand or impressive; and a model on duty announces she is holding a pose.

clue.text: A £1000 piano

explanation.surface: A piano priced at a thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand is slang for a thousand pounds; and a grand is a large concert piano.

clue.text: Back round part created for malevolent young stars

indicators.note: the word back goes round the other piece
the letters are newly made into another arrangement

explanation.surface: Writing a supporting role for a group of mean-spirited young actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' reads like a verb of support but is the outer word placed 'round' the scramble signalled by 'created'. The Brat Pack were a set of young 1980s Hollywood actors.
explanation.definitionFit: The name given to a group of brash young film actors of the 1980s.

clue.text: Sailor bursts into song in the country

indicators.note: the sailor letters break into the song word

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera
AB is able-bodied seaman, a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor breaks into song out in the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: Arabia is the peninsula and historic land of the Arabs.

clue.text: Silent order from the recruiting officer

definitions.text: Silent order from the recruiting officer

indicators.note: to order is to arrange, so these letters are put in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A recruiting officer silently commanding a recruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A recruiter's command to join up the armed forces.

clue.text: Army corps assumed to have been ransomed

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
deemed means considered or supposed

explanation.surface: A military unit presumed to have been freed by paying a ransom.
explanation.definitionFit: To ransom a captive is to buy back their freedom.
